o: A divisor k of n is sortable if we can sort the whole array by rotating each length-k block cyclically. Rotations never move elements between blocks, so block b of the final sorted array must contain exactly the same multiset as block b of the current array. In Example 1 ([3,1,2], n=3): k=1 fails because singleton blocks cannot reorder anything, while k=3 succeeds since one rotation sorts the array — answer 3. Example 2 fails for both divisors, giving 0. Example 3 is already sorted, so every divisor (1 and 2) counts, totaling 3. Checking each divisor takes O(n), and n has at most ~128 divisors, so total work is fine.
k: Rotation preserves each block's multiset, so k is sortable iff for every block b, sorted(block b) equals the corresponding slice of the globally sorted array.
Only divisors of n need checking; each check is O(n).

a.n: Approach 1: Check every divisor with block multiset comparison
a.i: For each divisor k, sort each block and compare with the matching slice of the fully sorted array. If all blocks match, rotations can realize the sorted order block by block.
s: For each k dividing n: for each block b, compare sorted(nums[b*k:(b+1)*k]) with s[b*k:(b+1)*k].
If every block matches, add k to the answer.
a.t: O(n·d(n)·log n) worst case with sorting per block; effectively O(n log n · d(n)) — fast since d(n) <= 128 for n <= 1e5.
a.sp: O(n) for the sorted copy and temporary blocks.

a.i: Assign each element its rank in the sorted order (stable for ties). Block b is correct iff it contains exactly ranks bk..bk+k-1, checked with a presence array per block — avoiding repeated sorting inside the divisor loop.
s: Sort a copy of (value, original index) to compute rank[index] for each position.
For each divisor k: for each block, mark seen ranks and verify the block's rank set equals {bk, ..., bk+k-1}.
a.t: O(n log n + n·d(n)) — one sort plus O(n) work per divisor.
a.sp: O(n) for rank and marker arrays.

w: Either approach passes comfortably; the rank-based one avoids repeated block sorting and is the cleaner asymptotics story. Pitfall: forgetting k = 1 is almost never sortable (blocks cannot reorder), and only testing divisors of n. Edge cases: already-sorted arrays (every divisor counts), n prime (only k = 1 and k = n candidates). Follow-up: allow swapping two blocks, or count sortable k for circular rotations of the whole array.
